message.content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) has, over the past two decades, [profoundly (and irrevocably) {transformed (the very (foundations [upon which] modern computational discourse rests))} the way scholars, engineers, and policymakers approach problems of escalating complexity, from protein structure prediction to stochastic climate modelling to the normative governance of autonomous decision-making systems]. This transformation is not merely incremental; it constitutes a paradigm shift in how the research community conceptualises the relationship between data, representation, and inference. Where early symbolic systems treated cognition as a hierarchy of rigid production rules, contemporary architectures—particularly those built upon deep generative modelling—expose the field to questions of interpretability, alignment, and epistemic responsibility that no prior generation of computational theory was equipped to answer.

The present paper contributes to this ongoing conversation by proposing a unified evaluation framework for assessing not only the predictive fidelity of large-scale language and multimodal models, but also the downstream cognitive and social effects of their deployment in high-stakes domains such as medical diagnosis, judicial reasoning, and scientific hypothesis generation. We argue that current benchmarking methodologies, which privilege accuracy and throughput, systematically underweight the probabilistic opacity and distributional fragility that characterise state-of-the-art systems, thereby creating a false sense of assurance in both academic and industrial contexts.

Our contribution is threefold. First, we formalise a multi-axial metric—what we term *cognitive surface transparency* (CST)—that quantifies the degree to which a model's internal representations can be mapped onto human-interpretable features without loss of predictive coherence. Second, we introduce a suite of adversarial and counterfactual probes designed to stress-test the boundary conditions under which model outputs remain calibrated. Third, we situate our findings within the broader trajectory of AI research, identifying specific theoretical gaps—particularly at the intersection of information geometry and causal inference—that remain unresolved and that, in our assessment, will constrain the next generation of architectures unless addressed at the foundational level.

The paper is organised as follows. Section 2 reviews the relevant literature, tracing the arc from connectionist foundations through the transformer revolution to the current landscape of foundation models and agentic systems. Section 3 presents the formal framework and its mathematical underpinnings. Sections 4 and 5 detail the experimental design and results, respectively, drawing on a corpus of 1.2 billion tokens spanning four languages and three scientific domains. Section 6 discusses limitations, ethical considerations, and broader implications for the governance of AI in the public sphere. Section 7 concludes with directions for future work.
